about: Companion to the files in ./locales. Nothing imports this at runtime — it exists so that whoever writes the next language (person or model) knows where a string appears, what it is allowed to say, and which jokes are meant to be replaced rather than translated.

scripts/checkI18n.ts enforces that it stays honest: every namespace in en.json needs an entry with a non-empty "where", every flavour-text list needs its own note, and every shipped locale needs an entry in languageNotes. Adding a namespace without documenting it fails the build.
howToAddALanguage: 1. Copy locales/en.json to locales/<code>.json and translate it. English is the reference: it's where the source strings are authored, and what checkI18n compares against.

2. Add one line to LANGUAGES in i18n/index.ts, labelled with the language's own endonym (Italiano, 日本語 — not "Italian", "Japanese"). resources, supportedLngs and the Settings picker are all derived from that array.
3. Add a languageNotes entry below, covering at least the plural shape and the register you chose.
4. Run `npm run check:i18n -w web`. It verifies key parity, interpolation parity per plural variant, and this file's coverage.

Plural shape is the one thing that bites. i18next looks up `key_<category>` for the target language and falls back to the bare `key` when that's absent. So: a language with only `other` (Japanese, Chinese) can use bare keys alone; a language with one/other (English, Italian) needs bare + `_other`, because a `_other`-only key resolves to the raw key name at count 1; and `_many` (Spanish, Italian, ≥1,000,000) falls back to the bare *singular* if omitted, which is why sync.offlinePending spells it out.

conventions.interpolation: {{name}}, {{count}}, {{days}}, {{age}}, {{months}}, {{version}} etc. are substituted verbatim. Keep every one the reference uses; word order may move freely around them. checkI18n compares the set per key, treating variables English omits from one plural variant as optional.
conventions.markup: diary.birthdayLine and birthdayLineWithAge contain a <mention> element rendered as a styled @mention chip. Keep the tag and its contents intact; move it within the sentence as the grammar needs.
conventions.sigils: @ marks a person and # marks a tag; both are typed literally into entry text and parsed by lib/tokens.ts. Never localise or space them away — "@人物" is correct, "@ 人物" is not.
conventions.brandNames: Google, WhatsApp, WeChat, Groq, OpenRouter, Cerebras, Markdown, Android, Tamagotchi and API key placeholders (gsk_…, sk-or-…, csk-…) stay as they are. WeChat may take its local name where one is standard (微信).
conventions.examplePlaceholders: Example phone numbers are localised to a plausible number for the language's main market, keeping the international format the hint is teaching. Email placeholders stay at example.com (an RFC-reserved domain).
conventions.ellipsis: Placeholders and in-progress labels use the single character … , not three dots.
conventions.length: These strings sit in chips, buttons and table cells. Aim at or below the English length; a chip truncates with an ellipsis rather than wrapping.

tone.default: Plain, warm, second person, no exclamation marks. This is a private diary, not a productivity tool — it should never sound like it is grading the user. Prefer the everyday word over the technical one, except in Settings where precision matters more.
tone.flavourText: notifications.dailyReminderBodies, notifications.birthdayBodies and people.checkupBodies are picked at random (see pickTemplate in lib/notifications.ts) and are the only deliberately funny strings in the app. Translate the *joke*, not the words: swap in a reference that lands in the target culture, and keep globally-recognised ones (Tamagotchi, achievement unlocked, breaking news) where they already work.
tone.flavourTextLimits: Tease, never scold or guilt-trip. The user has done nothing wrong by not writing for a few days. No streak-shaming, no implication that a friendship is failing, nothing about the user being a bad friend — nudge with affection. Keep them short enough to survive a lock-screen notification, roughly one or two short sentences.
tone.genderNeutrality: {{name}} is any person of unknown gender, and the reader's gender is unknown too. In gendered languages, avoid constructions that force agreement on either: prefer verbs and nouns that don't inflect, restructure rather than pick a default, and never ship a slash form (amico/a).

app.where: The name and one-line strapline, on the sign-in screen and in the browser/app title.

keys.name: The product name. Translated rather than kept as a brand — this is a personal app, not a trademark.

nav.where: Sidebar on desktop, bottom tab bar on phones. The tightest space in the app — one or two words, no verbs.

keys.diary: Labels the entry list; distinct from app.name so the tab can be shorter than the product name.
keys.threads: See the threads namespace for the concept and the term chosen per language.

auth.where: Sign-in screen, and the sign-out button at the bottom of Settings.

keys.continueWithoutAccount: Starts a local-only diary with no server account. Should sound like a real choice, not a downgrade.

sync.where: A status pill in the header, and toasts when the connection or session state changes.

keys.offlinePending: Counted. Very tight — it sits in a pill beside the header. "Offline" plus a count of queued changes.

update.where: A banner when a new app version is available.

keys.needsInstall: {{version}} is a semver string; keep the literal "v" prefix next to it.

notifications.where: System notifications (Android via Capacitor). Titles show on the lock screen, truncated hard; bodies get a little more room.

keys.dailyReminderTitle: Fires when nothing has been written today. Keep it under about 30 characters.
keys.dailyReminderBodies: Flavour text — a random one is picked each day. Ten variants, all on the theme "today is still blank". Replace the culture-specific ones freely: the Italian set nods to Nanni Moretti's Caro Diario, the Japanese to 三日坊主 (giving up on day three), the Chinese to 断更/催更 (a serialised story going quiet, and readers demanding the next chapter) and 打卡 (habit check-ins). Never scold — see tone.flavourTextLimits.
keys.birthdayTitle: The 🎂 is intentional and worth keeping; notification titles are otherwise plain text.
keys.birthdayBodies: Flavour text — seven variants nudging the user to send a message. Warm and celebratory, never guilt-inducing. "Confetti emojis" is worth localising to whatever people actually send: the Japanese set uses LINE スタンプ, the Chinese 撒花的表情.

common.where: Shared button and control labels across every dialog, form and toast.

keys.cancel: Dismisses a dialog. In several languages this is the same word as `undo`; that's fine, they never appear together (cancel is in dialogs, undo is in toasts).
keys.undo: The action button on a toast, reversing what just happened.
keys.less: Collapses an expanded list. Pairs with `more`; both must fit a small ghost button.
keys.optional: Lowercase on purpose — it renders inline beside a field label.

importance.where: The 1–5 importance picker on an entry, the Settings decay table, and the legend of the Markdown export.

keys.levels: Five ranks from 1 (life-changing) to 5 (routine). Single words or very short phrases; they sit beside a coloured dot in a narrow picker. They also drive how long an entry stays a talking point, so the ordering must read as clearly descending.
keys.descriptions: One line each, shown as help text. Concrete examples beat abstractions — localise the examples themselves ("moving abroad") if a different one is more relatable.

diary.where: The day view: the entry list, the composer, and the entry edit/delete dialogs.

keys.composerPlaceholder: Teaches the @ and # sigils. Keep both literal characters.
keys.willBeSaidTo: Labels checkboxes over the people an entry mentions. Creating an entry marks it as already told to whoever it mentions, and these let the user untick that.
keys.subEntries: Counted. Entries nest up to three levels; a sub-entry is a detail hanging off a parent entry.
keys.birthdayLine: Contains the <mention> element — see conventions.markup. Shown as a synthetic row in the day view on someone's birthday, not a real entry.
keys.createTag: Inline "create this one" row in the tag picker, with {{name}} being whatever the user has typed so far.

people.where: The people list, and every tab of a person's profile: talking points, events, memories, history. The largest namespace.

keys.talkingPoints: The core concept: things from the diary worth telling this person, ranked and decaying over time. Needs a term that reads as "things worth mentioning", not "agenda items" — Italian uses Spunti, Japanese 話のネタ, Chinese 谈资. It must not collide with the word chosen for threads.
keys.markSaid: Records that this entry has now been told to this person. The single most-pressed button in the app; keep it short enough for a small outline button.
keys.unmarkSaid: Reverses a said-mark, in the "Already told" list. Reads as a state ("not said yet"), not a command.
keys.hideForPerson: Suppresses one entry for one person forever. {{name}} is the person.
keys.matchMention: Badge explaining *why* an entry was suggested: it names the person directly. Sits beside matchTag and matchBroadcast in a narrow badge.
keys.matchTag: Badge: the entry and the person share a tag.
keys.matchBroadcast: Badge: the entry is broadcast to everyone regardless of match.
keys.checkupReminders: "Checkup" here means getting back in touch with someone after a while, not a medical check. Choose a word for reaching out, not for inspecting.
keys.checkupDueTitle: Notification title when someone is overdue. {{name}} is the person.
keys.checkupBodies: Flavour text — twelve variants, the funniest set in the app, shown when it's been {{days}} days since the user last told this person anything. Both {{name}} and {{days}} must appear. Localise the references: Tamagotchi is kept everywhere because it's globally understood (and native in Japanese, たまごっち); the read-receipt joke becomes visto e non risposto in Italian, 既読スルー in Japanese, 已读不回 in Chinese; "radio silence" becomes 音信不通 / 潜水. Absolute limit: affectionate teasing about the silence, never a suggestion that the user is neglecting a friendship.
keys.events: Things that happened *to* this person — a trip, an exam, surgery — which the app later reminds the user to ask about. Not calendar appointments, and not the user's own entries.
keys.eventFollowUpDescription: Shown when events have just finished. The tone is "ask them how it went".
keys.aliases: Extra names one person answers to, widening @mention autocomplete. "Other names" rather than "aliases" if that sounds less bureaucratic in the language.
keys.alsoKnownAs: An inline prefix before a nickname list. Very short; a gendered participle (Italian detto/detta) must be avoided here.
keys.phoneInternationalHint: Teaches the international format. The example number is localised per language — keep the leading + and the country code.
keys.wechatQrDescription: Explains a WeChat limitation: a chat can't be opened from a link, so the ID has to be pasted into WeChat's own search.
keys.birthdayInDays: Counted, shown as a countdown chip beside a name.
keys.ageYears: Counted, used both standalone and inside a birthday line.
keys.checkupsPending: Counted badge on the People nav item and the list header.

tags.where: The Tags management page, plus tag pickers throughout. Tags attach to both entries and people, and a shared tag is what makes an entry a talking point for someone.

keys.color: Tags are user-coloured; threads deliberately are not.
keys.usage: {{entries}} and {{people}} are counts of each. Rendered as one dense line under the tag name.

threads.where: The Threads page, the thread picker in the composer, the "Add to thread" dialog, and the grouped headers on a person's talking-points tab.

keys.title: A thread is a named group of entries about one ongoing topic spanning many days — a project, a house move, a research effort — so the whole topic can be caught up on in one action. Not a discussion thread and not a tag. Pick a word for a continuing storyline: Italian Filoni (as in filone narrativo), Japanese スレッド, Chinese 话题. Beware false friends — Chinese 线程 means a CPU thread. Must not collide with the word chosen for people.talkingPoints.
keys.toTell: Counted, in a thread's group header: how many of its entries this person hasn't been told yet. Extremely tight — it shares a row with the thread name and a button.
keys.markAllSaid: Marks every currently-suggested entry in this thread as told to this person, in one click. Fits a small button next to toTell.
keys.markedAllSaid: Confirmation toast. {{count}} entries in the thread named {{name}}.
keys.limitReached: {{count}} is the per-entry thread cap (MAX_THREADS_PER_ENTRY in shared/src/constants.ts).
keys.deleteConfirmDescription: Reassures that deleting a thread only ungroups: the entries and every said-mark survive. Worth keeping that reassurance explicit.

calendar.where: The month calendar and its day summaries.

keys.onThisDay: Entries written on this same date in previous years — any year, not specifically last year. Most languages have a set media phrase for this: Italian Accadde oggi, Chinese 那年今日, Japanese 過去の今日.

search.where: The search page, its filter panel and result count.

keys.from: A date-range start. Same word as markdownExport.from and people.eventStart in English, but each may differ per language — they're separate keys on purpose.

settings.where: The Settings page. The one place where precision beats warmth: several strings explain the scoring model, and a vague translation makes the controls unusable.

keys.decay: Explains half-life decay of talking points. "Half-life" is the literal physics term and should use the language's established one (emivita, 半減期, 半衰期) — the mechanic really is exponential decay.
keys.memories: Old entries about a person resurfacing as shared memories after a threshold age.
keys.broadcast: Suggesting an entry to everyone rather than only to matching people.
keys.checkups: Account-wide default for the per-person checkup interval.
keys.ai: Optional voice-to-entry assistant. Provider names and key prefixes are literal; apiKeyHint and its siblings end mid-sentence because a link follows in the UI — keep them ending in a way that a URL can follow.
keys.markdownExport: Exports part of the diary as Markdown intended to be pasted into an AI agent, not read as a backup.
keys.data: Backup, restore and export. "Backup" as a noun may stay a loanword where that's what people say.

keys.crash: The last-resort error boundary. Its job is to reassure that nothing was lost — keep the promise that entries are safe on the device.

entry.where: Error codes, not UI labels. The server returns these keys as-is (e.g. 'entry.not_found') and the client renders t(code), so the key names must never change — only the messages.

keys.max_depth: Raised when nesting an entry deeper than three levels.

person.where: Error codes returned by the server for people. See the entry namespace.

keys.duplicate_name: Two people can't share a name, because @mentions would be ambiguous. Worth hinting at the reason.

tag.where: Error codes returned by the server for tags. See the entry namespace.

keys.duplicate_name: Enforced by a unique index per account.

thread.where: Error codes returned by the server for threads. See the entry namespace.

keys.duplicate_name: Enforced by a unique index per account.

ai.where: The voice-entry button, its recording states, and the suggestion review dialog. Also the error codes the AI routes return.

keys.thinking: Shown while the model turns a transcript into draft entries. Deliberately vague about the model.
keys.acceptAll: Counted: adds all reviewed suggestions to the diary.
keys.invalid_key: "LLM" appears in these messages because the user supplies their own provider key and needs to know which thing failed. Keep it recognisable.

import.where: Importing people from the device address book (Android only). Its conflict wording is close to importBackup's but the two are separate flows and separate keys.

keys.conflictContainment: One name looks like a substring or variant of another, so they may be the same person. A suggestion, not a verdict.
keys.keepBoth: Creates a second person rather than merging.

importBackup.where: Restoring a JSON backup file, and its conflict-resolution review screen.

keys.sectionSummary: {{label}} is a section name taken from this same namespace (tags/threads/people/entries), so the sentence must work with any of them substituted in.
keys.overwrite: Replaces the existing entry in place, as opposed to addAsNew.
keys.done: Eight counts in one sentence. Feel free to restructure into clauses that read naturally; keep every placeholder.
keys.orphaned: Counted. An imported sub-entry whose parent wasn't imported gets promoted to the top level.

en.role: Reference language. Source strings are authored here and checkI18n compares every other locale against it.
en.plurals: one/other. Keys use the bare form for the singular plus `_other`.
en.register: Second person, contractions allowed, sentence case throughout — including buttons.

es.plurals: one/many/other. sync.offlinePending spells out all three; `_many` only matters from 1,000,000 and is omitted elsewhere.
es.register: Tú, never usted. Spain vocabulary (móvil, vale).
es.notes: The original language of the project — several English strings read as translations of these. Flavour text stays close to the English jokes.

it.plurals: one/many/other, same as Spanish. Bare form for the singular plus `_other`; `_many` given only for sync.offlinePending, matching the Spanish precedent.
it.register: Tu, informal. Sentence case. Guillemets «» for quoted names, matching Italian typographic convention rather than the straight quotes English uses.
it.gender: The hard constraint in this language. Both {{name}} and the reader have unknown gender, so several strings are deliberately restructured to dodge agreement: people.alsoKnownAs is "alias" rather than detto/detta; a checkup body says "al suo posto ci sia un Tamagotchi" instead of a participle agreeing with the person; "a {{name}} manchi" avoids inflecting on them entirely. Preserve that discipline when editing.
it.references: notifications.dailyReminderBodies quotes «Caro diario, oggi…», after Nanni Moretti's film. people.checkupBodies uses "visto e non risposto" (the seen-but-unanswered messaging culture), "colpo di scena", "Ultim'ora" and "Obiettivo sbloccato". Tamagotchi is kept.
it.terms: Entry = voce, sub-entry = sotto-voce, thread = filone, talking point = spunto, tag = etichetta, checkup = promemoria di contatto.

ja.plurals: Only `other` exists, so a single unsuffixed key covers every count and no `_other` variant is needed. Do not add `_one` — i18next will never select it, and a nicer singular wording (昨日終了 for "ended yesterday") is simply unreachable; people.eventEndedDaysAgo therefore uses the general 「{{count}}日前に終了」.
ja.register: です／ます, friendly but not stiff. Notifications lean casual with ね／よ endings. No 敬語 beyond that — this is the user's own diary talking to them, so humble/honorific forms would be wrong.
ja.counters: Counters are baked into the strings around {{count}}: 件 for entries and generic items, 人 for people, 個 for tags, 日 / 日間 for days, 歳 for age. Changing a noun means rechecking its counter.
ja.honorificOnNames: {{name}} is followed by さん in notifications and profile prose, which is the natural register. The trade-off is accepted knowingly: if a user stores a name that already ends in an honorific, it will double up. Names in this app are free text, most often given names, so さん is the better default.
ja.references: 三日坊主 (quitting on day three) for the daily reminder, 実績解除 and 段位 for the achievement joke, 既読スルー for the read-receipt joke, 音信不通 for radio silence, スタンプ (LINE stickers) in place of confetti emojis. たまごっち is kept and is native rather than a loan.
ja.typography: No spaces around 「」 or between Japanese and adjacent punctuation. A space goes either side of *literal* Latin runs (API キー) but deliberately not around interpolations: {{name}} may hold either a Latin or a Japanese name, and a hard-coded space would be wrong half the time. document.documentElement.lang is set on language change, which matters here — it tells the browser to pick Japanese rather than Chinese glyph forms for shared Han characters.
ja.terms: Entry = 記録, sub-entry = サブ記録, thread = スレッド, talking point = 話のネタ, tag = タグ, event = 出来事, checkup = 連絡リマインダー.

zh.script: Simplified (zh-Hans), targeting mainland usage. Registered as plain `zh`, so zh-CN/zh-SG resolve to it via nonExplicitSupportedLngs; a zh-Hant locale can be added later without touching anything else.
zh.plurals: Only `other` exists — single unsuffixed keys, exactly as in Japanese.
zh.register: 你, informal and direct. Sentence case is not a concept; keep punctuation full-width (：，。「」) except inside Latin runs.
zh.measureWords: Measure words sit around {{count}} in the strings: 条 for entries and talking points, 人 for people, 个 for tags and threads, 天 for days, 岁 for age, 件 for events. Changing a noun means rechecking its measure word.
zh.references: 断更／催更 (a serialised story going quiet, readers demanding more) and 打卡 (habit check-in) for the daily reminders; 电子宠物 for Tamagotchi; 已读不回 for the read-receipt joke; 潜水 for going silent; 表情包 and 「在吗」 for the send-something nudge; 成就解锁 for the achievement joke; 那年今日 for calendar.onThisDay.
zh.typography: A space goes either side of literal Latin runs and of numeric interpolations (Groq API 密钥, {{count}} 条记录) — standard Chinese typesetting, and what keeps an interpolated digit from fusing with a measure word. No space around {{name}}-style interpolations, though, since those may hold Han text and a hard-coded space would then be wrong. WeChat takes its local name 微信.
zh.terms: Entry = 记录, sub-entry = 子记录, thread = 话题, talking point = 谈资, tag = 标签, event = 经历, checkup = 联系提醒. Note 线程 was rejected for thread: it means a CPU thread.
